metric.core_tooling_availability_quality.evidence_sources: Official Rust documentation (The Rust Book, Cargo Book), rust-lang.org blog announcements, VS Code Rust docs, ArchWiki Rust page, rustup project documentation.
metric.core_tooling_availability_quality.proxy: Presence, first-party/official status, integration maturity, and de-facto-standard adoption of the core toolchain: compiler/runtime, official installer/toolchain-version manager, formatter, linter, language server (IDE backend), integrated build tool, integrated test runner, documentation generator, and debugger support.
metric.core_tooling_availability_quality.retrieval_route: web search against official docs/blog + third-party confirmation, same depth applied as for other languages in sibling shards
metric.core_tooling_availability_quality.scale: 90-100 = complete first-party toolchain, all core tools official and tightly integrated/shipped together, undisputed single standard, no fragmentation. 70-89 = core tools available and treated as standard but one or more components are third-party or loosely integrated. 50-69 = tools exist but the ecosystem is fragmented across competing options with no clear default. 30-49 = one or more core tool categories missing or immature. 0-29 = core tooling largely absent or unreliable.

metric.package_dependency_management_qua.evidence_sources: The Cargo Book (official), crates.io, lib.rs ecosystem statistics, GitHub rust-lang/crates.io-index.
metric.package_dependency_management_qua.proxy: Maturity of the package manager and its integration into the toolchain: lockfile-based reproducibility, semantic-versioning-based resolution, workspace/monorepo support, availability and scale/reliability of a central registry, and availability of security-auditing tooling.
metric.package_dependency_management_qua.retrieval_route: web search against official Cargo Book pages plus registry-statistics sites, same depth applied as for other languages in sibling shards
metric.package_dependency_management_qua.scale: 90-100 = fully integrated first-party package manager with lockfiles, semver resolution, workspace support, a mature large-scale registry, and security tooling. 70-89 = solid package manager but missing one dimension (e.g., no native workspace support, smaller registry). 50-69 = functional but fragmented package management (multiple competing tools, weak lockfile guarantees). 30-49 = significant gaps in reproducibility or registry maturity. 0-29 = no standard package manager or registry.

Rust.gaps_noted: Debugging support relies on wrapper scripts around external native debuggers (gdb/lldb via rust-gdb/rust-lldb) rather than a dedicated first-party Rust debugger, and profiling tooling (e.g. cargo-flamegraph, perf integration) is largely third-party; this keeps the score below the top of the band despite an otherwise complete first-party suite.
Rust.rationale: Rust ships a complete, first-party, tightly-integrated toolchain distributed through a single official installer.
raw_evidence: <cite index="6-13,6-14">rustup is the official installer and version manager for Rust, installing rustc, cargo, clippy, rustfmt, and the standard library in one command.</cite>
<cite index="6-6">Always install Rust via rustup; it's the official, supported method.</cite>
<cite index="5-2">Clippy is included with standard Rust installations.</cite>
<cite index="5-6">Rust installations include rustfmt by default, so you should already have the programs rustfmt and cargo-fmt on your system.</cite>

<cite index="4-1,4-2">When you install Rust with rustup, the toolset includes the rustc compiler, the rustfmt source code formatter, and the clippy Rust linter, along with Cargo, the Rust package manager.</cite>
<cite index="35-2">The rust-analyzer project, a new implementation of the Language Server Protocol (LSP) for Rust, is now officially a part of the wider Rust organization.</cite>

<cite index="36-1,36-3">The Rust Language Server (RLS) is being deprecated in favor of rust-analyzer, with builds of RLS continuing until at least the Rust 1.64 release, after which no new releases will be made.</cite>
<cite index="36-10">In RFC 2912 rust-analyzer was adopted as the official replacement for RLS.</cite>
<cite index="6-12">rust-analyzer is the Rust Language Server; it powers IDE features (autocomplete, go-to-definition, inline errors) in VS Code, JetBrains, Neovim, etc.</cite>
<cite index="2-14,2-15">IntelliJ IDEA has a Rust plugin, and the same plugin also works with CLion.</cite>

<cite index="9-27,9-34,9-37">rustup component add is used when a tool ships with the official toolchain, like rustfmt or clippy; the rustup command manages the compiler and its companions, and when you switch Rust versions, rustup switches these tools too, preventing version drift.</cite>
Rust.score_basis: Meets the top band (90-100) criteria: complete first-party toolchain (rustc, cargo, rustup, rustfmt, clippy, rustdoc, rust-analyzer) shipped/managed together with no fragmentation and undisputed single-standard tools; docked a few points for the debugger/profiler gap noted above.

Rust.data_quality_note: Registry size figures differ slightly across sources (327,112 crates indexed by lib.rs vs. ~193k reported by a third-party aggregator), reflecting different counting methodologies (e.g., inclusion of yanked/historical versions); both indicate a large, actively maintained registry and are reported here as a declared limitation of the popularity-count proxy rather than a single standalone score driver.
Rust.rationale: Cargo is a first-party, deeply integrated package manager backed by the large, actively used crates.io registry, with lockfiles, semver-based resolution, and workspace support.
raw_evidence: <cite index="12-1">Cargo downloads your Rust project's dependencies and compiles your project.</cite>

<cite index="7-12">Cargo streamlines dependency management, automates build processes, and facilitates publishing and sharing of crates through crates.io, the official registry for Rust packages.</cite>
<cite index="27-3">The result of the resolution is stored in the Cargo.lock file which "locks" the dependencies to specific versions, and keeps them fixed over time.</cite>
<cite index="27-9">Cargo uses SemVer for specifying version numbers.</cite>
<cite index="20-12">When building multiple packages in a workspace (such as with --workspace or multiple -p flags), the features of the dependencies of all of those packages are unified.</cite>

<cite index="19-14,19-15">Yanked releases are those that are marked that they should not be used, and when the resolver is building the graph, it will ignore all yanked releases unless they already exist in the Cargo.lock file.</cite>
<cite index="11-9,11-10,11-11">There are 72,022 users or teams that have a crate on crates.io, growing at a rate of 1.4x per year, and Lib.rs has indexed 327112 crates.</cite>
<cite index="11-1">crates.io has served 1500.0 million downloads in a single day, which is more than all downloads in the first 52 months since the release of Rust 1.0 in May 2015.</cite>
<cite index="13-1">The crates.io package index contains the necessary metadata for cargo to download crates and resolve their dependencies.</cite>
<cite index="9-32">Third-party security tools such as cargo-audit are installed and run via cargo install, integrating into the standard Cargo workflow.</cite>
Rust.score_basis: Meets top-band criteria: fully integrated first-party package manager, Cargo.lock reproducibility, semver resolution with feature unification, native workspace support, and a large-scale, high-traffic central registry (crates.io) with community security-auditing tooling; not a perfect 100 because some auditing/supply-chain tooling (cargo-audit, cargo-deny) remains third-party rather than bundled by default.

evidence.scope_note: This shard evaluates only the Rust language for the two assigned metrics under the Toolchain/Developer Ecosystem Maturity category. Other languages are scored by sibling shards; the runner merges disjoint language keys per metric.
